items.title: Newton's biggest theorem says integration and differentiation are inverses
items.claim: Define F(x) as the area under f from 0 to x. The derivative of F is f. Define G(x) as an antiderivative of f. Then integral from a to b of f dx = G(b) - G(a). Two operations that look unrelated are inverses.

options.text: Integration (continuous summation) and differentiation (instantaneous rate) seem like different operations — but they undo each other. This is one of the most surprising and powerful results in mathematics

items.reveal:
Two parts:

FTC Part I: If f is continuous on [a, b] and F(x) = integral from a to x of f(t) dt, then F is differentiable on (a, b) and F'(x) = f(x).

FTC Part II: If f is continuous on [a, b] and G is any antiderivative of f (so G'(x) = f(x)), then integral from a to b of f(x) dx = G(b) - G(a).

Geometric intuition for Part I: F(x) is area under the curve up to x. As x increases by a small amount dx, the area increases by approximately f(x) * dx — the height at x times the width dx. So dF/dx = f(x).

Why it's surprising:
- Differentiation computes a LOCAL rate at one point.
- Integration sums up TOTAL accumulated value across a range.
- The connection: knowing the total at every point tells you the rate; knowing the rate everywhere tells you the total.

Applications:
- Definite integrals become easy: find an antiderivative, plug in endpoints, subtract.
- Areas, volumes, work, charge, total amounts of accumulated quantities — all computable via antiderivatives.
- Differential equations: solving f' = g is equivalent to finding an antiderivative of g.

Historical: Newton (~1665) and Leibniz (~1675) both discovered it independently. It's the cornerstone of mathematical physics.

Before the FTC, calculating areas under curves (the 'quadrature problem') was a major mathematical challenge — Archimedes computed parabola areas through laborious limit arguments. After the FTC, antiderivatives reduce the problem to algebra.
items.why: Calculus has two halves that look unrelated. The fundamental theorem reveals they are inverses — the same way logarithm and exponential are inverses. This unification is the most powerful idea in elementary mathematics.

items.title: Just 23 people give a 50/50 chance of a shared birthday
items.claim: How many people do you need in a room for it to be more likely than not that two share a birthday? Most people guess 100 or 180. The answer is 23.
items.prompt: Why is the threshold so low?

options.text: With 23 people there are 23 choose 2 = 253 possible pairs, each with about a 1/365 chance of matching; the question is not 'matches me' but 'any match anywhere', which has many more chances
Coincidences happen because of cosmic alignment

items.reveal:
The probability that NO two people in a group of n share a birthday is (365/365)(364/365)(363/365)...((365-n+1)/365).

For n = 23, this product equals about 0.493. Probability of AT LEAST ONE match equals 1 - 0.493 = 0.507. Just over 50 percent.
For n = 41, probability of a match is about 90 percent.
For n = 70, about 99.9 percent.

Intuition fails because we ask 'does someone share MY birthday?' — that requires n ≈ 253 for 50 percent. The real question allows ANY pair to match, and the number of pairs grows as n choose 2 ≈ n squared / 2.

This 'birthday attack' is important in cryptography: collision resistance of a hash function with N possible outputs only protects against attackers who try fewer than about square root of N inputs. A 128-bit hash gives only 64-bit collision security.
items.why: Counting pairs is qualitatively different from counting people. Pair counts grow quadratically, so coincidences are far more likely than a head-count suggests.

items.title: sin(1 degree) is irrational
items.claim: Sine of 30°, 45°, 60° are simple expressions like 1/2, sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(3)/2. Sine of 1 degree, 7 degrees, or most other 'nice' integer degree values are irrational numbers with no closed elementary form.
items.prompt: Why are most integer-degree sine values irrational?

options.text: Niven's theorem (1956): the only rational values of sin(theta) for rational theta in degrees occur at multiples of 30 (giving sin = 0, plus/minus 1/2, plus/minus 1). Almost all other rational-degree sines are irrational

items.reveal_title: Niven's theorem and the gaps in trigonometric tables
items.reveal:
Ivan Niven (1956) proved: if both theta (in degrees) and sin(theta) are rational, then sin(theta) is 0, ±1/2, or ±1. By similar argument, cos(theta) rational with theta rational forces cos(theta) in {0, ±1/2, ±1, ±sqrt(2)/2... wait — Niven's actual statement covers SINES specifically}.

The consequence: sin(1°), sin(2°), sin(3°), ... are mostly irrational. Specifically, the standard table of integer-degree sines contains only a few rational values: sin(0°) = 0, sin(30°) = 1/2, sin(90°) = 1, and their reflections (150°, 210°, 270°, 330°). Every other entry in the table is irrational.

This is one reason the SPECIAL ANGLES (30°, 45°, 60°) feature so heavily in geometry: they have simple exact values. Most other angles need decimal approximations.

Closed-form expressions: many integer-degree sines do have closed forms in terms of nested radicals — they're algebraic numbers — but the expressions are ugly. For example, sin(15°) = (sqrt(6) - sqrt(2))/4. sin(18°) = (sqrt(5) - 1)/4 (related to the regular pentagon).

For sin(1°): expressible in radicals (it's algebraic, a root of an integer polynomial) but the expression has dozens of nested terms. Modern algebra has tools to compute it exactly; it's just not a useful form.

Why 30° and 45° are special: regular hexagons (60° angles) and squares (45°) tile the plane with simple geometric constructions; the corresponding sine/cosine values come out as simple radicals.

Gauss and constructibility: a regular n-gon is constructible with compass and straightedge if and only if n is a product of powers of 2 and distinct Fermat primes (3, 5, 17, 257, 65537). This is why the 17-gon is constructible (Gauss's first major result, age 19) but the 7-gon and 9-gon aren't.
items.why: Trigonometric tables look like they could be filled with simple values. Almost all entries are deeply irrational, expressible only in nested radicals or numerical approximations. The 'special angles' of school maths are a tiny privileged set.
